result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.bfs()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Perform breadth-first search (BFS) traversal from a start node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L18340-L18440){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.bfs( start, attr_name=None, return_list=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Breadth-first search](/assets/graphs/algo-bfs.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph explored by BFS from a source on the left. The source and its two distance-one neighbors are shown in the accent color; the two distance-two nodes in a lighter accent tint; and the furthest distance-three node in default styling. BFS tree edges are highlighted in accent; the two non-tree same-layer edges are drawn in default." width="100%"} BFS explores the graph layer by layer, visiting all neighbors of a node before moving to their neighbors. Can return the visit order as a list, or store the position of each node in the traversal as a node attribute for visualization. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [start]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Starting node (integer ID or string label). [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store traversal position. If `None`, uses `bfs_order` as the attribute name. Position is 0-indexed (start node = `0`, first neighbor = `1`, etc.). Nodes not visited get no attribute set. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns list of node IDs in visit order. If `False`, stores positions as node attributes and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[list[int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=` is `True`: list of node IDs visited in BFS order. If `return_list=` is `False`: returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A binary tree makes the level-by-level nature of BFS easy to see, since every node at a given depth is visited before the traversal moves on to the next level: ::: {#8cf86e7a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_balanced_tree(k=2, h=3) visited = graph.bfs(start=1) # Returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, ...] (level by level) visited ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` Number of nodes : 15 Number of edges : 14 Directed : False Density : 0.13 Average degree (min, max) : 1.87 (1, 3) Connected : True Number of connected components : 1 Tree : True Bipartite : True Computations on nodes: - bfs(start=1) -> attr: 'bfs_order' (15 of 15 nodes) ``` ::: ::: Instead of returning a list, `bfs()` can stash each node's visit position as an attribute, which is convenient for driving a visualization (e.g. sizing nodes by how early they were discovered): ::: {#83654201 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_balanced_tree(k=2, h=3) .bfs(start=1, return_list=False) .rescale_node_attrs( node_attr_from="bfs_order", node_attr_to="size", range=[0.5, 2.0] ) ) # The root is discovered first, so it gets the smallest size graph.get_node(1).attributes["size"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0.5 ``` ::: ::: The traversal works the same way on a 2D grid, expanding outward layer by layer from the starting corner: ::: {#2090569f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_grid_2d(3, 3) # Start from the top-left corner (0, 0) visited = graph.bfs(start=1) visited ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Number of nodes : 9 Number of edges : 12 Directed : False Density : 0.33 Average degree (min, max) : 2.67 (2, 4) Connected : True Number of connected components : 1 Tree : False Bipartite : True Computations on nodes: - bfs(start=1) -> attr: 'bfs_order' (9 of 9 nodes) ``` ::: :::
